snippet.title: ai morning #17 — etched exits stealth with $800m and a bet that gpus are the wrong tool
snippet.description:
An AI inference chip startup nobody had heard of came out of stealth with $800 million raised. Over a billion dollars in customer contracts were already signed. Its team is mostly ex-NVIDIA engineers. The pitch: GPUs are the wrong tool for inference at scale.

Marcus walks through what Etched actually built, why Andrej Karpathy betting against the GPU he taught the world to use is the signal worth watching, and what it means for builders pricing out agent infrastructure.

In this episode:

00:00 Intro
01:28 Etched: $800M chip, Karpathy bets — Inference startup exits stealth with $1B+ in contracts and a team of 400 ex-NVIDIA engineers backed by Hinton, Thiel, and Karpathy.
02:57 OpenAI's 5% stake pitch — Altman reportedly offers the US government equity in an $852B company, while Godot's maintainers ban AI PRs after the review queue breaks.
04:46 Autonomy: agents that run without — agency-agents hits 124K stars, GLM 5.2 jumps 32 ranks on OpenRouter, and Qwen AgentWorld reframes the model as an environment simulator.
06:09 GPT-5.6, Gemini Omni Flash, Claude — GPT-5.6 global release whispered for next week, Gemini Omni Flash reportedly in preview, and Claude Desktop Linux beta rumored today.

snippet.title: AI's 3 big narrative violations — 7/2/2026
snippet.description:
Three things the market believed about AI broke this week.

One: you have to own the model. The whole race was about building the best frontier AI — until Meta this week said its building a cloud business to sell off its excess computing power. The stock jumped. The message: maybe the money was never in the model, especially as this layer commoditizes. Investor Dan Niles joins to break down what Meta's move means for the whole AI trade.

Two: AI is coming for jobs. New data from Ramp and Revelio Labs — covering more than 21,000 US companies — cuts against the story everyone expected. The firms spending hardest on AI aren't shrinking their headcount. They're growing it. Ara Kharazian, lead economist at Ramp, and Garrett Lord, CEO of Handshake, on what the jobs data actually shows and whether it holds.

Three: open source can't make money. The assumption was that giving your model away for free meant no business. That's breaking too, as open-model companies start posting real revenue and enterprises move from renting AI to running their own. Vipul Ved Prakash, CEO of Together AI, and Clément Delangue, CEO of Hugging Face, on where the money goes when the best models are cheap and open.
